name: TPS62130RGTR
title: TPS62130, TPS62130A, TPS62131, TPS62132, TPS62133: 3 V to 17 V input, 3 A synchronous step-down converters in 3 mm × 3 mm VQFN-16
summary: A family of synchronous buck converters with both power MOSFETs inside a 3 mm × 3 mm 16-pin VQFN (RGT). They run from 3 V to 17 V and deliver up to 3 A; the TPS62130 and TPS62130A are adjustable from 0.9 V to 6 V on a 0.8 V feedback level, while the TPS62131, TPS62132 and TPS62133 are fixed at 1.8 V, 3.3 V and 5 V. DCS-Control switches at about 2.5 MHz (or 1.25 MHz, picked on the FSW pin) and slides into power save mode at light load, with 17 µA typical quiescent current and 1.5 µA in shutdown. Soft start and tracking on SS/TR, an open-drain power-good output, a DEF pin that raises the output 5 %, 100 % duty cycle, current limiting and thermal shutdown are built in.
key_figures: 800 mV typ, 785.6 mV to 814.4 mV in PWM
about 2.5 MHz (FSW low) or 1.25 MHz (FSW high)
90 mΩ high side, 40 mΩ low side typ at VIN ≥ 6 V

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node, joined inside to both power MOSFETs. The inductor connects between this pin and the output capacitor.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power-good output: high (released) when the output is in regulation, low when it is below its nominal level. Needs a pull-up resistor.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input of the adjustable versions, taken from a resistor divider on the output. On the fixed versions it is best tied to AGND, which helps thermal performance.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Analog ground. Tie straight to the exposed pad and the common ground plane.

pins.name: FSW
pins.function: Switching frequency select: low gives about 2.5 MHz, high about 1.25 MHz. For the high setting tie it to VOUT or PG. Pulled low inside when left floating.

pins.name: DEF
pins.function: Output voltage scaling: low regulates to the nominal output, high to nominal plus 5 %. Pulled low inside when left floating.

pins.name: SS/TR
pins.function: Soft-start and tracking. A capacitor on this pin sets how fast the internal reference ramps up; a voltage driven onto it makes the output track that voltage, for sequencing.

pins.name: AVIN
pins.function: Supply for the control circuits. Feed it from the same source as PVIN.

pins.name: PVIN
pins.function: Supply for the power stage. Feed it from the same source as AVIN.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable: high turns the converter on, low turns it off. Pulled low inside when left floating.

pins.name: VOS
pins.function: Output voltage sense input for the control loop.

pins.name: PGND
pins.function: Power ground. Tie straight to the exposed pad and the common ground plane.

pins.name: EP
pins.function: Joins AGND (pin 6), PGND (pins 15, 16) and the common ground plane. It has to be soldered for the rated power dissipation and for mechanical strength.

circuits.title: Typical application, 1.8 V output
circuits.description: A fixed-output 1.8 V, 3 A regulator: VIN feeds PVIN, AVIN and EN together, so the part runs whenever input is present. 10 µF and 0.1 µF sit across the input, 3.3 nF on SS/TR sets the start-up ramp, and the inductor with 22 µF forms the output filter, with VOS sensing at the output node. FB, DEF and FSW go to ground (nominal voltage, 2.5 MHz), and 100 kΩ pulls PG up to the output.

circuits.title: 3 A point-of-load converter
circuits.description: The reference design the measurements are taken with: VIN feeds PVIN, AVIN and EN, C1 (10 µF) and C7 (0.1 µF) decouple the input, C5 (3.3 nF) on SS/TR sets the soft-start ramp, L1 and C3 (22 µF) form the output filter with VOS sensing at the output, R1 and R2 set the output voltage, R3 (100 kΩ) pulls PG up to the output, and DEF and FSW are grounded.
notes: R1 and R2 are chosen for the wanted output voltage with the output-voltage equation.
Parts used for the typical-characteristic measurements: L1 XFL4020-222MEB (2.2 µH), C1 10 µF 25 V 1210, C3 22 µF 6.3 V 0805, C5 3300 pF 25 V 0603, C7 0.1 µF 25 V 0603, R3 100 kΩ 0603 1 %.

circuits.title: Single power LED supply
circuits.description: The converter drives one power LED at constant current. The LED sits between the output and FB, and a 0.1 Ω resistor from FB to ground senses its current. A 187 kΩ resistor from SS/TR to ground, fed by the 2.5 µA SS/TR current, lowers the feedback target to about 300 mV, so the sense drop stays small; a voltage applied on ADIM at SS/TR dims the LED. Input runs from 4 V to 17 V with 10 µF and 0.1 µF decoupling, the inductor is 2.2 µH and the output capacitor 22 µF.

parts.note: sets the FB level from the SS/TR current

notes: VFB = 0.64 × 2.5 µA × RSS/TR gives the feedback level; the LED current is that level over the 0.1 Ω sense resistor.
Analog and PWM dimming are both supported; this circuit was tested with analog dimming.

circuits.title: Output discharge through PG (TPS62130A)
circuits.description: The TPS62130A version in the standard adjustable circuit, with R3 from the output to PG. In normal running R3 is the PG pull-up; when EN, UVLO or thermal shutdown turns the part off, the TPS62130A holds PG low and the output capacitor drains through R3. The size of R3 sets how fast the output falls.
notes: Current into PG stays under 10 mA.
PG stays low only while VIN is present.

circuits.title: -3.3 V inverting supply
circuits.description: The TPS62130 wired as an inverting buck-boost: the inductor's far end is system ground, and the IC's ground pins, DEF, FSW and the feedback divider return to the negative output, which sits at -3.3 V. One 10 µF capacitor runs from VIN to system ground and another from VIN to the -3.3 V rail; 0.1 µF from AVIN to the rail and 3.3 nF on SS/TR complete the IC side. 1.21 MΩ and 383 kΩ set the output, a Schottky diode runs from the -3.3 V rail to ground, 22 µF filters the output, and a resistor pulls PG up to system ground. Input runs from 3 V to 13.7 V, so VIN plus the output magnitude stays within 17 V.
notes: The loop now carries a right-half-plane zero; at least 22 µF of output capacitance is recommended.

operation.text: The regulation loop mixes hysteretic, voltage-mode and current-mode ideas: an AC path from the output goes straight to a fast comparator, which fixes the steady-state switching frequency and reacts at once to load steps, while a voltage feedback loop holds the DC level accurate. Compensation is internal, so small parts and low-ESR capacitors work. One block covers both PWM and power save mode, so passing from one to the other leaves no mark on the output. The fixed-output versions need just four external parts; an internal current limit allows up to 3 A of nominal output current.

At medium and heavy load the part runs in continuous conduction at a nominal 2.5 MHz or 1.25 MHz, chosen on FSW; the actual frequency shifts in a controlled way with VIN, VOUT and the inductance. It stays in PWM while the output current exceeds half the inductor ripple current, and changes over to power save mode where the inductor current would turn discontinuous. When VIN falls to roughly 15 % above VOUT the part stays in PWM whatever the load.

At light load the inductor current goes discontinuous and the part enters power save mode on its own, dropping the switching frequency in proportion to the load to keep efficiency high. Pulses use a fixed on-time; very low output voltages keep at least about 80 ns, which pulls the frequency below nominal, and at high duty cycle the off-time can hit its minimum, with the output still regulated. Quiescent current in this mode is about 17 µA.

As VIN approaches VOUT the duty cycle rises until the high-side switch stays on continuously, with the low-side FET off. It remains on as long as the output sits below its set point, which lets a battery-fed rail run down to a very small input-output difference.

When the high-side current reaches the limit the high-side FET turns off and, after a pause against shoot-through, the low-side FET conducts so the inductor current falls. The high side turns on again only once low-side current has dropped below the low-side limit, about 3.5 A typical. If the output falls below 0.5 V the part treats it as a short and cuts the limit to about 1.6 A; above 0.5 V it returns to normal. Propagation delay lets the real peak current exceed the static limit, most at high input voltage with small inductors.

EN high starts the converter; EN low shuts it down, drawing about 1.5 µA, with both power MOSFETs and all control circuits off. The internal divider then lets the output fall gently. EN should be driven high or low; an internal pull-down of about 400 kΩ holds the pin low if it was low and then floats, and is switched out once EN goes high. Driving EN from another rail's output sequences several supplies.

After EN goes high the part waits about 50 µs, then the output rises at a slope set by the capacitor on SS/TR, which limits inrush current and keeps weak sources from sagging. A very small capacitor, or none, gives the fastest start; there is no upper limit on start-up time. Starting into a pre-biased output is allowed: neither power MOSFET switches until the internal ramp passes the pre-bias level. Below about 0.5 V on the output the current limit is cut to about 1.6 A. Shutdown, undervoltage lockout and thermal shutdown each pull SS/TR low through an internal resistor, and leaving any of them begins a fresh start-up.

Driving SS/TR with an external voltage makes the output follow it up and down; between 50 mV and 1.2 V on SS/TR, FB sits at about 0.64 times that voltage. Once SS/TR reaches about 1.2 V the reference clamps at the normal feedback level and ordinary regulation takes over. Since the part cannot pull current out of the output, on a light load the output can fall more slowly than SS/TR. SS/TR must stay within VIN + 0.3 V. If VIN drops into undervoltage lockout or to zero, the output goes to zero whatever the tracking voltage. Below its 0.8 V typical value the FB accuracy may be wider than specified.

PG of one converter wired to EN of the next gives sequential start-up. Two converters sharing one soft-start capacitor start ratiometrically. Feeding the second converter's SS/TR from the first output through a divider R1/R2 lets its ramp run faster, slower or at the same rate as the first.

PG is an open-drain output that needs a pull-up to any voltage under 7 V; it holds its specified low level while sinking 2 mA. It is released when the output reaches regulation and pulled low when it is below. On the TPS62130 PG goes high-impedance when EN, UVLO or thermal shutdown turns the part off; the TPS62130A holds PG low in those states instead, which can discharge the output, as long as VIN remains. An unused PG pin should go to GND but may float.

DEF high raises the output 5 % above nominal; DEF low gives the nominal value. The pin's maximum is 7 V, so it is tied to VOUT or PG rather than VIN. An internal pull-down of about 400 kΩ keeps a floating pin low after it was set low, and is disconnected once the pin is driven high.

FSW low gives about 2.5 MHz for the smallest filter parts and lowest ripple; FSW high halves the frequency to about 1.25 MHz for better efficiency at the cost of more output ripple. The part must start with FSW low to limit inrush, which tying FSW to VOUT or PG achieves. At the lower frequency an inductor of at least 2.2 µH is recommended for low ripple and full current. The frequency may be changed while running; the pin has the same switched 400 kΩ pull-down as DEF.
When the input falls through the UVLO threshold, about 2.7 V typical, both power FETs are turned off. The converter restarts once the input climbs about 200 mV above the threshold.

An internal sensor watches the junction. Above about 160 °C both power FETs turn off and PG goes high-impedance; when the junction cools by the hysteresis of about 20 °C the converter starts again with a soft start.

The TPS62130 and TPS62130A set their output with a divider from VOUT to AGND, between 0.9 V and 6 V, with FB regulated to 800 mV. The TPS62131, TPS62132 and TPS62133 have the divider inside; their FB pin is pulled down internally and may float, though tying it to AGND improves thermal resistance. For the lowest current draw the fixed versions are preferred. If FB comes open the output at VOS is clamped internally at about 7.4 V.

The inductor and output capacitor form a double pole that sets the converter's corner frequency, so they are chosen together within the range the internally compensated loop accepts; a set of nominal pairings is proven stable in simulation and lab test. Inductance can go as low as 1 µH with FSW low; with FSW high or at low input voltage 2.2 µH is recommended.

The inductor value sets ripple current, output ripple, the PWM-to-PSM transition and efficiency; its saturation current and DC resistance must suit the load. Its saturation rating should cover the maximum inductor current at the real operating conditions plus about 20 %. A larger inductance lowers ripple but slows transient response and grows the part.

22 µF is the recommended output capacitance. Small low-ESR ceramics in X5R or X7R are recommended for low ripple and stable capacitance over temperature and frequency. A larger value lowers ripple and tightens DC accuracy in power save mode, where the ripple is set by capacitance, ESR and inductor peak current together.

10 µF of low-ESR multilayer ceramic, placed as close as possible between PVIN and PGND, suits most designs; more lowers input ripple current. AVIN and PVIN share one source, but a separate 0.1 µF from AVIN to AGND is required against noise coupling. An RC low-pass from PVIN to AVIN is allowed but not needed. Ceramic capacitance falls with DC bias, depending on case size, voltage rating and dielectric, so the effective value must be checked.
A capacitor from SS/TR to AGND, charged by a constant 2.5 µA, sets the output's start-up slope; CSS = tSS × 2.5 µA / 1.25 V sets it for a wanted ramp time tSS.

Both fixed and adjustable versions carry an internal 25 pF capacitor from VOS to FB, which forms a zero and a pole with the feedback divider. The part is stable without placing them anywhere in particular, but moving them, or adding an external feed-forward capacitor, can improve power-save behaviour and transient response.

The TPS62130 can drive a power LED by putting a sense resistor in the FB path and lowering the FB target through a resistor on SS/TR, which the 2.5 µA SS/TR current turns into a voltage. The part then regulates its output, the LED anode, to hold a constant current. Analog and PWM dimming both work. The minimum input voltage must cover the LED's forward voltage.

Because the TPS62130A pulls PG low when EN, UVLO or thermal shutdown turns it off, a resistor from PG to VOUT discharges the output in those cases; the same resistor is the PG pull-up in normal running and sets the discharge rate. Current into PG must stay below 10 mA.

With the external circuit rearranged, the TPS62130 makes a negative output. The IC's ground then sits below system ground, so VIN plus the output magnitude must stay within the 17 V maximum supply. The transfer function gains a right-half-plane zero, so the loop needs adapting and at least 22 µF of output capacitance is recommended.
The input source must supply 3 V to 17 V and be rated for the current the output voltage and load demand.

Layout matters greatly at these switching frequencies; a poor one degrades line and load regulation, stability and accuracy, and raises EMI and noise sensitivity. AGND and PGND both connect directly to the exposed pad, which in turn connects to the ground plane. VOS runs by the shortest route to VOUT at the output capacitor, routed apart from the output power trace. Switched-current paths are short and wide, input and output capacitors sit close to the pins, and loops carrying AC current enclose as little area as possible. FB and VOS stay short and away from SW and other fast-edged nodes, sensing at the output capacitor. The SS/TR and AVIN capacitors and the FB resistors R1 and R2 sit close to the IC with direct connections to their pins and the ground plane. The exposed pad must be soldered.

The maximum junction temperature in operation is 125 °C, so output power is limited by the losses the package and board can carry away. More copper around the part, wide thick top-layer traces and vias under the IC into inner ground layers lower the thermal resistance; soldering the exposed pad and adding airflow also help. Overload and short circuit are covered by internal limiting of the power dissipation. Measurements on the TPS62130 evaluation module give the highest ambient temperature that keeps the junction at or below 125 °C without airflow or heatsink.
